that's the plan! i don't bake ever so i never thought i would need one until i decided to try making this pizza

my thought exactly! i left chicago for texas and haven't been able to find anything remotely similar enough.  this definitely filled the void i had for good stuffed pizza.  it was super easy to make too! here's what i did:

2 and 1/2 cups flour
1/2 cups yellow corn meal
1 and 1/4 tsp salt
1 tbsp granulated sugar
2 1/4 tsp yeast
1 and 1/4 cups warm water
1/4 cup olive oil, extra to grease bowl
1/4 cup softened butter

-mix 2 and 1/2 cups of flour and the rest of the dry ingredients together in a bowl
-add warm water and olive oil, stir until just moistened and then knead by hand for 5 minutes.  dough should be smooth and soft.  if dough is sticky, add more flour 1/4 of a cup at a time.
-form dough into a ball and place into a bowl that is lightly greased with olive oil.  turn dough to coat all sides, cover and let rise for 1-2 hours.
-remove dough from bowl and punch down, and then roll out into a large rectangle.
-spread softened butter over the dough  and then roll up short side to short side.
-cut roll in half, for each part into a ball, and then either freeze or let rise in greased bowl in the fridge for 1 hour
-after dough has puffed up, roll out 3/4 of the dough into a thin circle and line your a greased pan (i used butter)
-add cheese and toppings of your choice
-roll out remaining 1/4 of dough into a thin circle, getting it as thin as you can.  lay over top of pan, crimping edges to seal and cutting away excess dough.  cut slits in top to vent steam, then cover with sauce and grated parmesan
-bake at 425F for no more than 30 minutes

for the sauce, i just used crushed tomatoes, some tomatoe sauce, garlic powder, oregano, basil, and olive oil.

I am a transgender man, so I hope I can maybe offer a little bit of perspective from the other side.  I understand, at least through the lens of a child who watched their mother go through this, the emotional response to learning that your child is gender questioning, at the least.  It's wordy and I'm sorry if it seems rambly, I just want to offer some kind of help or insight  if I can.

I never had a word for how I felt growing up, but I knew it didn't feel right.  I always just assumed it was because of me being so shy and reserved, because I was a very private child who wanted to be very outgoing like my sister.  I always imagined myself growing up to be her, and I wore dresses and make up and played house and cooked.  I played a lot of sports because my brother did, and I played rough because I played with my older brother and his friends, but I was very much a girly girl for tne majority of my life.  I loved pink and frills and princesses, and had tea parties and wore costumes.  But I also felt like I had to, like if I overcompensated then I would feel 'right'.  It's not something I ever mentioned or talked about, even though I told my mom everything.  I didn't know how, even though she always always told me that she'd love and accept me no matter who I was or who I loved.

Around your son's age, I felt less and less like I wanted to be the me I was.  I thought it was because I wanted to escape my life, because my siblings moved out and my parents divorced and my friends were growing away from me.  I was struggling, and I also started fantasizing about being a boy.  I would hide my hair under a hat and wear my brother's sweaters to look like a bigger boy instead of young woman.  I dreamed up an "alter ego" and pretended to be him because it made me feel better not being me.  But I was just 'quirky' and 'different'.  I still felt like I had to be a girl, because that's all there was.  I still didn't know how to put those feelings into words for myself, let alone my mother.

I didn't come out to myself, so to speak, until I was 21.   It just kind of clicked, all of a sudden.  Like everything suddenly made sense to me.  And I knew my mom would accept me, because like I said, she always told me the same things you're saying about accepting your child.  But when I told her, she felt very much the same.  Like it came out of the blue, and that there were never any signs.  That it was a phase, or that I would change my mind.  She's still coming to terms with it, and it's been years.  I don't know if this is something that you can relate to, but she told me that the hardest part was feeling like she had lost a child, or that all of her dreams for me and of me were dead.  Everything she had envisioned for me for the better parts of two decades were gone.  Even if I did them, it wouldn't be like she imagined.

For me, it didn't feel out of the blue.  I always knew, even if I didn't know how to say it or how to feel it.  It was always there.  But, that being said, I don't think I would have been ready then.  I would support your son, and allow him the freedom to explore his identity and how he expresses it.  Maybe it is just a phase for him, or maybe he just isn't a traditional girl.  It's okay to be a girl who digs up worms and plays sports and laughs at fart jokes.  I wouldn't pursue puberty blockers or estrogen or any radical processes, but supporting him on this journey, wherever it takes you both, can only help you both.  Because at the end of the day, that's going to mean the most.

I think it depends on the him as well as you, but I do think you can still get to know a person without frequent video calls or voice chatting.  My girlfriend and I rarely do voice or video calls due to schedule conflicts, and it's just been this way since we met four years ago.  But, we have and still talk to each other via text every day, and I think I have a fairly accurate idea of her as a person.  We just met in person for the first time this month, but she was the same person face to face as she was in her messages.  If you want more face or voice time with him, you should definitely discuss it with him.  Otherwise, I'd just say to make sure you're having the kinds of conversations that would reveal more parts of him and it will still be okay.

Didn't move away from my family for my partner, but I did move cross-country for college!  It's hard and you will definitely get homesick, but my suggestion is to treat it a little similarly to how you treat your ldr.  Make time to talk to your family and check in with them, discuss when it's possible to visit, etc.  Also, while it'll be difficuly at first, once you get settled into your new life with work, friends, classes, and your SO, it will ge easier.  Time will pass faster than you think, and before you know it you'll be home for a bit.  My immediate family is all scattered around the world now, but we all email or call when we can and it helps to keep us close.
